newsitem.title: DUBAI: Some officials in Tehran for Afghan meet.
newsitem.headline: Some officials in Tehran for Afghan meet.

text.p: Officials from the United Nations, Turkey, India and the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) have arrived in Tehran for a regional conference Iran is hosting on Tuesday to seek a solution to the Afghan crisis.
The official Iranian news agency IRNA late on Monday reported the arrival of the officials in Tehran, and said some had met Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati.

Iran said on Friday it had invited Russia, India, Pakistan, China, Saudi Arabia and the Central Asian states to attend the conference. Also invited are the European Union and the 52-nation OIC, which groups most of the world's Moslem nations.
Pakistan has said it would not attend, but it was not immediately clear if any of the remaining countries invited were taking part in the two-day conference.

IRNA had this week quoted visiting Russian officials as saying Moscow was sending a delegation to the conference. It also said the ousted Afghan government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, which Iran supports, would take part.
It quoted Velayati as saying on Monday the conference was a new effort by Iran to end the Afghan crisis and bring "the position of the regional countries closer together..."
It said U.N. envoy Francis Okelo told Velayati the conference "was a fundamental step towards universal efforts for returning peace to Afghanistan."

"He (Okelo) expressed hope that as the result of Iran's efforts, clashes in Afghanistan would come to a halt and that the Afghan groups would agree to the formation of a broad-based government," IRNA added.

Okelo was sent to Iran by U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl, who has been trying to broker a ceasefire between the Islamic Taleban movement and its foes after the Taleban forced out the government from Kabul in September.
Pakistan said on Sunday it would not attend the conference citing problems with the agenda and guest list, which includes arch-rival India.

Pakistan and Iran have been working closely together in diplomatic moves over Afghanistan during 17 years of civil war there, but differences appeared between them after the emergence of the Taleban as a new factor in Afghan politics.
Iran's media have accused Pakistan of setting up the Sunni Moslem Taleban with backing from the United States and funding from Saudi Arabia to counter Iran's influence in the region.
Pakistan denies the charge and says it has no favourites among the Afghan factions.
Iran last week blasted the Taleban as "rebels" and reiterated its recognition of Rabbani's government.
